title: Rain intensity, seasonality, PET and the IPO did not explain 1902-2025 changes in runoff at equal rain at 18 south-east Australian gauges; cool-season rain loss explains 1/3 of the 2010-2025 deficit
abstract:
Question: in long Bureau of Meteorology flow records, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff at equal annual rain was high before about 1957, low in the 1960s-1990s and low again after 1997 (bundle 4e9ae7e7). Do measured climate covariates explain this multi-decadal variation with the same coefficients that hold from year to year before 1997, and do they also predict the post-1997 deficit?

Approach: 18 SE-AU gauges (8 cells of 2 x 2 degrees), annual panel model 100Q/Qbar = a + bP + cP(t-1) + z beta, calibrated before 1997. Covariates: daily heavy-rain share and wet-day count from a fixed network of 145 GHCN-D stations, May-October rain share (SILO), CRU TS 4.09 PET and the IPO tripole index (ERSST v5). Cross-validated 13-year blocks; 2,000-draw cell bootstrap. Plan and decision rules were written before any residual was calculated.

Results: heavy-rain share had no clear effect (beta +0.34% of mean flow per share point, -0.56 to +1.00) and explained no block variation (CV R2 -0.01) or post-1997 deficit; this held for four alternative intensity indices. All five terms gave block CV R2 0.25 (-0.43 to 0.70); the 1941-1953 surplus (+17.6%) had a climate part of +2.5%. The 2010-2025 departure was -13.8% (-25.7 to -4.5); the five-term climate part was -1.5% (11%), and only the cool-season share contributed clearly (-4.4%, -6.9 to -1.9; 32%) after it fell to its lowest values of the record. The IPO predicted a small surplus. By the planned rules, rain intensity does not explain the variation, the five-term result is partial, and the state-shift reading was not met. Post hoc, the pre-1957 surplus of a gauge did not predict its 2010-2025 deficit (Spearman -0.10, n=16), while 1997-2009 and 2010-2025 deficits agreed (+0.73) and were larger in flatter catchments with less soil water storage.

Conclusion: measured climate, including daily rain intensity, does not explain century-scale SE-AU runoff efficiency; cool-season rain loss is a partial cause of the post-2010 deficit; the early surplus and the late deficit appear to be different processes.

Limitations: only 5 usable 13-year blocks and 8 cells, so intervals are wide; unmeasured climate (orographic rain pattern, sub-daily rain) and early flow rating errors are not excluded; the cross-catchment test is post hoc.
